analysis.one_liner: Protects remaining old-growth federal forests in three Pacific states from logging, road-building, and mining.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 132 House cosponsors and three days of subcommittee hearings, but never reached a floor vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a National Ancient Forest Reserve System out of the remaining old-growth federal forests in Washington, Oregon, and California, banning logging, road construction, mining, and mineral leasing inside the reserves. It would also temporarily protect any other qualifying old-growth forest in those states until Congress drew permanent boundaries. The findings in the bill say less than 2 percent of the nation's forest remains old-growth and that continued cutting would destroy nearly all of it within a decade.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who use and depend on these forests: hikers, anglers, and hunters, Native Americans who use the forests for religious practice, downstream communities that rely on forest watersheds for clean water, commercial and sport salmon fisheries, and future generations. The bill's findings describe the forests as the last habitat for threatened and endangered species and a source of clean water, recreation, and scientific value.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hikers, anglers, salmon fisheries, future generations

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a National Ancient Forest Reserve System and permanently protects designated old-growth lands in Washington, Oregon, and California from timber sales, road building, tree cutting, mining, and mineral and geothermal leasing.

Extends the same protections, on an interim basis, to all other federal forest land in the three states that qualifies as ancient or associated forest, until Congress enacts forest-by-forest designations.
Requires agencies to reduce annual timber sale offerings by the volume of timber protected, and shifts the burden of proof to the government in disputes over interim-protection actions.
Orders a scientific study of the biological requirements for the survival of old-growth ecosystems, with recommendations for wildlife corridors and buffer zones due by January 1992.

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry and timber-dependent towns in the Pacific Northwest, which would lose access to a large share of federal old-growth timber, along with mill workers and logging contractors whose jobs depend on those sales. Mining and mineral-lesing interests would lose access to lands withdrawn under the bill. The bill's own findings acknowledge that Northwest timber cutting rates would have to drop substantially.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber companies and Northwest logging towns

drawbacks.text: The bill would sharply reduce the supply of federal timber in Washington, Oregon, and California, cutting income in timber-dependent communities and mill towns; the bill itself concedes Northwest timber cutting rates must fall substantially to sustain the resource.

The interim protection in Section 6 is a blanket prohibition: until Congress acts, every qualifying old-growth tract in three states is managed as a reserve, with no roads and no timber sales, and the burden of proof for any exception rests on the government, which critics would call an overly rigid approach that leaves local forest planning no role.

The bill bars native insect and disease suppression and most fire suppression inside reserves, accepting fire as a natural process, a choice that could raise risks to adjacent private property, though the bill permits suppression to protect life and property nearby.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would permanently preserve one of the country's most scarce and non-renewable natural resources at a real, concentrated cost to logging families and timber towns in the Northwest. The ecological case is strong — old-growth forest does not regenerate after logging for centuries — but the bill's blanket interim protections and heavy reliance on nationwide restrictions rather than forest-by-forest planning would have hit Northwest timber communities hard, and an honest supporter would pair it with transition assistance for affected workers and towns.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two committees, got three days of hearings in its subcommittees in July 1990, and then was superseded by a separate ancient-forest bill (H.R. 5295); neither version reached a House floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Jim Jontz introduced the bill on April 4, 1990, and 132 House members — 114 Democrats and 18 Republicans — signed on as cosponsors.
The bill was referred jointly to the Agriculture Committee and the Interior and Insular Affairs Committee, and later to subcommittees in both, which held hearings on July 24, 26, and 27, 1990.

On September 13, 1990, the action record points to H.R. 5295, and the bill never advanced past its subcommittees; no floor vote occurred in the House or Senate before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber industry and the Northwest logging economy came out ahead: no restrictions passed, old-growth logging continued under existing policy, and the substitute bill cited in the record also failed to become law in this Congress.

for.name: Jim Jontz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ancient Forest Protection Act and recruited its original 25 cosponsors.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee with joint referral over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 4, 1990 and never reported it out; its Forests Subcommittee held hearings but the bill was pointed to a separate bill (H.R. 5295) and died in committee.

against.name: House Interior and Insular Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill the same day and its National Parks and Public Lands Subcommittee held hearings in July 1990, but the full committee never voted on it.

against.name: Timber industry
against.role: Wood products companies and logging interests in the Pacific Northwest
against.what_they_did: Actively opposed restrictions on old-growth logging on federal lands during the 1990 spotted owl debate, pressing for continued timber supply from national forests.

against.name: George H.W. Bush administration
against.what_they_did: The administration opposed broad logging bans on Northwest federal forests and sought exemption processes for the northern spotted owl under the Endangered Species Act during 1990.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but skewed Democratic — 114 of 257 House Democrats versus 18 of 175 House Republicans — and the sharpest opposition came regionally from timber-state interests rather than strictly along party lines.

industries.note: The bill would ban timber sales and road building on designated old-growth lands and reduce annual federal timber sale offerings across three states. Its gain would come from continued access to public old-growth timber at public expense.

industries.industry: Recreation and tourism in the Pacific Northwest
industries.note: Preserved old-growth forests would keep intact the hunting, fishing, and recreation experiences the bill describes as unique and growing in demand.
The bill's findings state that wild salmon and steelhead runs depend on clean water from ancient forest watersheds, which logging degrades.
Reserve lands would be withdrawn from entry under the mining, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing laws, ending new claims inside the reserves.
